{{nihongo|'''Unaguhime Shrine'''|宇奈岐日女神社}} is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|Q845945|qid=Q845945}} located in {{ill|Yufu|Q990455|qid=Q990455}}, {{ill|Ōita Prefecture|Q133924|qid=Q133924}}. It is a {{ill|Shikinaisha|lt=Shikinaisha|qid=Q134917286}}, and under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|Q712534|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|lt=former shrine ranking system}}, it was classified as a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Prefectural shrine}}.   {{nihongo|'''Unaguhime Shrine'''|宇奈岐日女神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Bungo Province]].

It is also called “{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Rokushogu}},” and is commonly known as “Yufu Shrine” or “Yufusan Shrine.”  

== Enshrined Deities ==
The shrine enshrines the following six deities. The alternate name “Rokushogu” derives from worshipping these six deities:  

* {{ill|Kuni-no-Tokotachi|lt=Kunitokotachi-no-Mikoto|Q478504|qid=Q478504|lt=Kuni no Tokotachi no Mikoto}}  
* {{ill|Kunisatsuchi-no-Mikoto|Q5966692|qid=Q5966692}}  
* {{ill|Hoori|Q1051960|qid=Q1051960|lt=Hikohohodemi no Mikoto}}  
* {{ill|Ugayafukiaezu|Q1373935|qid=Q1373935|lt=Hikonagisatake Ugayafukiaezu no Mikoto}}  
* {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|ar|الإمبراطور جينمو|arz|الامبراطور جينمو|as|জিম্মু|az|Cimmu|bcl|Emperador Jimmu|be|Імператар Дзіму|ca|Jinmu|cdo|Sìng-ū Tiĕng-huòng|ckb|ئیمپراتۆر جینمو|cs|Džimmu|de|Jimmu|el|Αυτοκράτορας Τζίμου|eo|Imperiestro Jinmu|es|Jinmu Tennō|et|Jimmu|eu|Jimmu enperadorea|fa|امپراتور جینمو|fi|Jinmu|fr|Jinmu|hak|Sṳ̀n-vú Thiên-fòng|he|ג'ימו, קיסר יפן|hi|सम्राट जिममु|hr|Jinmu|hu|Dzsinmu japán császár|id|Jimmu|it|Jinmu|ja|神武天皇|jv|Jimmu Tenno|ka|ძიმუ|ko|진무 천황|kw|Emperour Jimmu|la|Jimmu|lt|Imperatorius Džinmu|lv|Džimmu|mn|Эзэн Хаан Жиммү|mr|जिम्मू|ms|Maharaja Jimmu|my|ဂျင်းမူ ဧကရာဇ်|nl|Jimmu|no|Jimmu|pl|Jimmu|pt|Jimmu|ru|Император Дзимму|sh|Car Jimmu|simple|Emperor Jimmu|sl|Cesar Džinmu|sr|Џинму|sv|Jimmu|th|จักรพรรดิจิมมุ|tl|Emperador Jimmu|tr|Jimmu|uk|Імператор Дзімму|uz|Jimmu|vi|Thiên hoàng Jimmu|war|Emperador Jimmu|wuu|神武天皇|zh|神武天皇|zh_classical|神武天皇|zh_min_nan|Sîn-bú Thian-hông|zh_yue|神武天皇|qid=Q200188|lt=Kamuyamato Iwarehiko no Mikoto}} (First Emperor Jimmu)

== About Unaguhime ==
[[File:Yufuin Basin 11.jpg|thumb|250px|right|{{ill|Yufuin Basin|Q11577584|qid=Q11577584}} (from the summit of {{ill|Mount Yufu|Q705288|qid=Q705288}})<br/>The basin was once a lake, said to have been developed by Unaguhime.]]  

Although the currently enshrined deities are the six listed above, the shrine name recorded in the {{ill|Engishiki|Q1342448|qid=Q1342448}} {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932|lt=Register of Shrines}} is “Unaguhime Shrine,” and the conferment of divine ranks in the Six National Histories was made to “Unaguhime no Kami (Unagihime no Kami).” Therefore, it is believed that the original deity was '''Unaguhime''' (also read Unagihime or Unakihime).  

Regarding the name “Unaguhime,” one theory holds that “unagu” refers to a necklace such as magatama beads, suggesting that a female chieftain shaman wearing such ritual ornaments later became deified. Another theory derives the name from “unagi” (eel).  

There is an old legend concerning Unaguhime that the {{ill|Yufuin Basin|Q11577584|qid=Q11577584}} was once a lake (the “Kerisaki legend”). According to this story, Unaguhime, the deity of Mount Yufu, saw the lake spread before her and ordered a strong man to kick through its shore. When he did so, the water drained away and the lake became a basin, through which the present-day {{ill|Ōita-gawa|Q11432686|qid=Q11432686}} now flows. The strong man was named “Michinomi no Mikoto” and is still enshrined at the subsidiary Kerisaki Gongen Shrine. It is also said that the remnant of the dried lake became {{ill|Lake Kinrin|Q11648024|qid=Q11648024}}.  

However, archaeological and geological evidence has not confirmed the lake legend. Pottery has been excavated from the basin floor, wooden fragments dating back 23,000 years were discovered 20–30 meters underground, and no diatomaceous earth—expected if it had been a lake—has been found.  

As for the interpretation of the tradition, some identify Unaguhime with “Hayatsuhime,” mentioned in the {{ill|Bungo no Kuni Fudoki|Q11633698|qid=Q11633698}}, while others point to the {{ill|Hime-Hiko System|Q11330202|qid=Q11330202}}. A similar tradition is also told of Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto in the Aso region.  

According to the ancient document {{ill|Uetsufumi|Q11360118|qid=Q11360118}}, discovered in Oita Prefecture (Kamakura period, authored by {{ill|Ōtomo Yoshinao|Q11433255|qid=Q11433255}}, the first lord of Bungo Province, and generally considered a forgery), Unagihime was a deity governing cotton cultivation. The area was called Yufu (meaning cotton), suggesting that cotton was once cultivated there.  

However, cotton was introduced to Japan in the 8th century, and before that, “yū” (wooden cotton) usually referred to cloth made from tree fibers such as paper mulberry or hemp.  

---

== History ==

== Founding ==
According to shrine tradition, the shrine was founded in the 12th year of the reign of {{ill|Emperor Keikō|Q329723|qid=Q329723}}. The “Shrine Register” records that Emperor Keikō conducted rituals here during his western expedition, and that in the third year of his reign, Hayatsuhime founded the shrine by imperial command.  

The shrine stands at the southwestern foothills of Mount Yufu. Historical sources indicate that it was originally established with Mount Yufu as its sacred object of worship (shintaisan).  

Another theory suggests that the shrine began with worship of eels as spirits based on the lake legend and later merged with the worship of Mount Yufu’s deity.  

== Overview ==
The shrine first appears in official history in 849 (Kashō 2), when it was granted the Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade, and in 883 (Gangyō 7), it was promoted to Senior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade. These ranks were conferred upon “Unaguhime no Kami.”  

In the mid-Heian period, the {{ill|Engishiki|Q1342448|qid=Q1342448}} {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932|lt=Register of Shrines}} lists “Unaguhime Shrine” in Hayami District, Bungo Province, classifying it as a {{ill|Shikinaisha|lt=Shikinaisha|qid=Q134917286}}.  

Until the {{ill|Edo period|Q184963|qid=Q184963}}, it was syncretized with {{ill|Bussan-ji Temple|Q11385308|qid=Q11385308}} under the system of {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|Q2279088|qid=Q2279088|lt=Shinto-Buddhist syncretism}}, but following the {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|Q1970535|qid=Q1970535}}, it assumed its present form. In 1873 (Meiji 6), it was designated a village shrine under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|Q712534|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines}}, and in 1923 (Taishō 12), it was promoted to prefectural shrine status.  

== Divine Ranks ==
* 849 (Kashō 2), 6th month: Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade (recorded in the {{ill|Shoku Nihon Kōki|Q1041301|qid=Q1041301}}) – listed as “Unaguhime no Kami.”  
* September 2, 883 (Gangyō 7): Promoted from Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade to Senior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade (recorded in the {{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|Q1052981|qid=Q1052981}}) – listed as “Unagihime no Kami.”  

---

== Shrine Precincts ==
The precincts exceed 10,000 tsubo and were once surrounded by ancient {{ill|Cryptomeria|Q147388|qid=Q147388}}, but many were destroyed by a {{ill|Typhoon|Q140588|qid=Q140588}} in 1991 (Heisei 3).  

The main hall is a vermilion {{ill|Nagare-zukuri|Q210684|qid=Q210684}} style structure. A large torii gate also stands in central Yufuin.

== Subsidiary Shrines ==

'''Within the precincts'''  
* Tadasu Shrine  
* Itsukushima Shrine  
* Otoshi Shrine  

'''Outside the precincts'''  
* Ogo Shrine  
  * Location: Kawaminami, Yufuin-chō, Yufu City  
  * The grounds contain many giant cedars, including the nationally designated natural monument “Great Cedar of Ogo Shrine,” over 1,000 years old and 38 meters tall (designated August 9, 1934).  

* Kerisaki Gongen Shrine  
  * Location: Nakagawa, Yufuin-chō, Yufu City  
  * Enshrines the deity associated with the Kerisaki legend.
